newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tung tells Kohl he confident of post-97 Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Tung tells Kohl he confident of post-97 Hong Kong.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, under attack at home and overseas for plans to tighten civil liberties laws after the handover to China, put his case for change to German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday.
Kohl held talks with Tung shortly after arriving from New Zealand, and aides said they discussed Hong Kong's future beyond its transition to China at midnight on June 30.
Tung has sparked angry opposition for his plans, which include requiring demonstrators to get police permits for protests and prohibiting foreign funding for political parties.

Hong Kong's future leader, who will take over the helm in 53 day's time, argues the changes are no stricter than existing restrictions in many developed countries and were needed to preserve stability for the territory's 6.4 million people.
Kohl told reporters after the meeting he was confident that China would stick to its treaty obligations to maintain Hong Kong's freedoms and capitalist way of life intact.
The pledges were codified in the 1984 Sino-British treaty on the transition and spelt out in the Basic Law, the China-promulgated constitution for post-colonial Hong Kong.
Pro-democracy legislators have angered Tung by campaigning actively in Hong Kong and abroad against the proposed changes.

Also high on their list of concerns is China's plan to install an interim provisional legislature in place of the elected chamber, undoing the democratic reforms sponsored by outgoing British governor Chris Patten that angered Beijing.
Tung, a former shipping tycoon selected for the post in December, has hit out at his opponents for painting a gloomy picture about Hong Kong despite business sector confidence.

Martin Lee, leader of the popular Democratic Party, who will lose his seat when China disbands the elected legislature, recently undertook an exhaustive trip to Europe and the United States to lobby against Tung's plans.
The trip culminated in a meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Tung lashed out at Lee for "badmouthing" Hong Kong abroad but cancelled his own tentative plans to visit North America, saying he was too busy.
Lee said he was disappointed that he did not get to meet Kohl to express his fear of Hong Kong's freedoms being eroded.

"He met the Hong Kong governor and future chief executive Mr Tung and neither of them was elected by Hong Kong people," Lee told reporters after a meeting with German members of parliament accompanying Kohl on his trip.

"I told them about, principally about, my concerns about... our freedoms when we are going to have this appointed legislature and it's already beginning to pass laws, rolling back human rights protection laws, and that the rule of law is not the same again because the legislature is not democratically elected by the people."

Kohl met Patten for 1-1/2 hours before embarking on a two-hour Chinese lunch and a shopping trip in Hong Kong's antiques quarter to the astonishment of passers-by, including a group of German tourists.

The controversial provisional legislature is due to meet in the Chinese border town of Shenzhen on Saturday to discuss the outcome of a three-week consultation exercise in Hong Kong that sought the views of people on Tung's proposed changes.
A key Tung aide said earlier this week he expected some of the proposed changes to be softened slightly but not abandoned altogether.
Kohl is due to depart from Hong Kong, the third leg of an Asia-Pacific tour to drum up support for German business, on Saturday morning.
